paras: The lynching of John Figures and Cicero Green took place on the night of July 21, 1885, when about one hundred armed men on horseback rode into Minden, Louisiana, and shot the two Black prisoners to death inside the town jail. The two men were held on accusations of murder, and the mob also took a number of townspeople prisoner, among them a local newspaper editor. The killing was carried in Louisiana papers and in brief wire items as far away as Nevada and Rhode Island.

Figures and Green were confined in the Minden jail, described in one wire item as "colored prisoners accused of murder." None of the reports names the person they were accused of killing or gives the circumstances of the charge.

According to the Weekly Thibodaux Sentinel, the citizens of Minden saw about a hundred armed horsemen appear in their streets at around eleven at night. The men went first to the sheriff's house but did not find him at home. They forced everyone they met to fall into line with them and went to the jail, which they had the jailer open.

The cells themselves stayed shut, because the absent sheriff had the keys in his pocket. By the Sentinel's French-language account, the men lit a candle and ordered the prisoners to hold up Figures and Green, one after the other, at the level of the cell door's crossbars, and then riddled them with bullets. A wire version printed in Nevada said instead that the men "forced open the door" of the jail and fired into the cell until they had filled both men "with buckshot," then rode away.

Throughout the raid the horsemen held as prisoners every citizen who appeared on the scene. One of them was Moses Fort, editor of the Democrat Tribune, who was held for several hours before being released.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of any of the armed men appears in the coverage, and none of them was named. About ten days later, a Shreveport dispatch reported that Henry Jackson, a Black man accused of killing a saloon keeper at Minden Junction, had been moved from the Minden jail to Shreveport because the people of Minden wished "to evade another lynching in their town like that of a few days ago."

The fullest accounts came from Louisiana weeklies dated August 1. The Madison Times in Tallulah gave the date and the number of men and treated the detention of editor Fort lightly, writing that the men "concluded to 'Hold the Fort'" for several hours. The Thibodaux Sentinel ran the story in French under the headline "Execution sommaire en Louisiane" and called the victims "meurtriers," or murderers, without qualification.

Outside the state the event appeared only as single sentences in news-summary columns. The Weekly Elko Independent in Nevada described the dead as "notorious negro desperadoes," while a "South and West" column that ran in the Narragansett Herald and, on August 5, the Abbeville Press and Banner of South Carolina called them "colored prisoners accused of murder." None of these items commented on the killing, and no Black-press coverage of it was found.

Accounts differ on how the mob got into the jail: the Thibodaux Sentinel said the jailer opened it on the mob's order, while the wire items said the men "forced open the door" or "forcibly entered." The Louisiana account, the most detailed and closest to the scene, also says the cells were never opened, so that the prisoners were shot through the bars.

accounts.label: Louisiana press (Madison Times)
accounts.gist: One hundred mounted armed men entered Minden on the night of July 21, killed two jailed negroes, and held townspeople including editor Moses Fort prisoner for several hours.

accounts.label: Louisiana press (Thibodaux Sentinel, French)
accounts.gist: About a hundred horsemen sought the sheriff, forced everyone they met into line, had the jailer open the jail, and, unable to open the cells, ordered prisoners by candlelight to hold Figures and Green up to the door bars one after the other and riddled them with bullets.

accounts.label: Wire report (western)
accounts.gist: One hundred armed men forced open the jail door Tuesday night and filled the two 'notorious negro desperadoes' with buckshot in their cell.

accounts.label: Wire report (South and West column)
accounts.gist: A crowd of men forcibly entered the Minden jail and shot to death two colored prisoners accused of murder.

framing.detail: The Madison Times gave a factual brief and joked that the men 'concluded to "Hold the Fort"' with the editor they captured; it offered no comment on the killings.
The Thibodaux Sentinel headed its account 'Execution sommaire en Louisiane' and called the victims 'meurtriers' (murderers), presenting the accusation as fact.
The Elko Independent's wire item called the victims 'notorious negro desperadoes', adopting the mob's characterization.
The 'South and West' wire column carried a one-line item calling them 'colored prisoners accused of murder', run in Rhode Island and South Carolina.
A Shreveport dispatch in the Vicksburg Commercial Herald referred to the killing as 'another lynching' that Minden wished to avoid repeating.
